problem: By 2018, embodied navigation research had produced many incompatible task definitions, testbeds and evaluation protocols, so methods could not be compared. Common problems included: ending an episode as a success when the agent merely came near the goal, measuring proximity with Euclidean distance, leaving sensor assumptions unstated (e.g., perfect odometry/GPS), and not quantifying how much the agent had been exposed to the test environment (some protocols trained for days or weeks on the test scene).
motivation: Shared task definitions and evaluation protocols (the 'common task framework', e.g. PASCAL VOC and ImageNet) drove rapid progress in computer vision. Navigation was seeing a surge of work across simulators (SUNCG/MINOS, AI2-THOR, Matterport3D, Gibson, ViZDoom, DeepMind Lab, CARLA), and without coordination this diversity would hinder progress. A working group of authors from many navigation labs therefore wrote down consensus recommendations.
key_idea: Standardize embodied navigation evaluation through a goal taxonomy, explicit reporting of sensors and of prior exposure to the test environment, a mandatory DONE/stop action, geodesic-distance success, a single primary metric SPL = (1/N) Σ S_i · ℓ_i / max(p_i, ℓ_i), and shared standard scenarios on SUNCG, Matterport3D, AI2-THOR and Gibson.
insight: SPL puts success and path efficiency into one interpretable number. Examples from the paper: 50% success on optimal paths gives 0.5; 100% success with paths twice the optimal length also gives 0.5; 50% success with p_i = 2ℓ_i gives 0.25. It is deliberately stringent, and the authors expect about 0.5 to be good performance in unseen complex environments, ideally calibrated against human SPL. Two further requirements matter: success must be judged only when the agent emits DONE, so reaching the goal by chance does not count, and distance must be geodesic, so a goal on the other side of a wall is not 'close'. Generalization claims are only meaningful if prior exposure to the test environment is quantified. The paper defines three regimes: no prior exploration, a pre-recorded exploration trajectory, and a time-limited exploration budget, with performance reported as a function of budget along a Pareto front. There are no experiments or ablations.
method: Goal taxonomy: PointGoal (coordinates), ObjectGoal (category), AreaGoal (room type); goals may also be specified by images or natural language, and instance-specific variants are allowed; sensory inputs (RGB, depth, haptics, maps, perfect odometry/GPS) must be stated explicitly.

Generalization regimes: no prior exploration; pre-recorded third-party exploration trajectory; time-limited agent-controlled exploration budget (e.g., 500 m, 1,000 m, 2,000 m) reported as an exploration–navigation trade-off; exploration can itself be evaluated by coverage within a path-length budget.

Rec. 1–2: a dedicated DONE action ends the episode and the agent is evaluated at that moment; if DONE is never emitted the episode fails; proximity uses geodesic (shortest-path) distance, not Euclidean.

Rec. 3 SPL: binary success S_i (within threshold τ = 2× agent body width, 0.4 m default; for AreaGoal, center of mass inside the area) weighted by ℓ_i / max(p_i, ℓ_i), averaged over N episodes. Suggested auxiliary measures: final distance to goal, SPL swept over τ, distribution of normalized path length, infractions/collisions, actuation time and energy.

Rec. 4–6 (simulators): continuous state spaces, SI units (1 unit = 1 m), documented and open-sourced simulator customizations, and open-source sim-to-real deployment software (e.g., ROS packages mirroring the simulator API).

Standard scenarios: SUNCG 500 single-floor houses (300/100/100); Matterport3D 61/11/18. For both, body width 0.2 m, τ = 0.4 m, and >100 start–goal configurations per scene with geodesic distance ≥ 1 m. AI2-THOR 120 scenes (20/5/5 per category) with PointGoal and ObjectGoal (navigation-only or interaction-based; success = object visible within 1 m), 125 scenarios per test scene. Gibson tiny (25/5/5), medium (100/20/20) and full (402/85/85) partitions with 100 start–goal pairs per space.
Rec. 7: the structure of the agent's internal representation (reactive → recurrent memory → map/topological memory) is central, and should be studied openly rather than prescribed.

setting.backbone: N/A (evaluation-protocol / position paper; no agent proposed)
setting.observation: not fixed; paper requires explicit reporting of sensors (RGB, depth, haptics, maps, odometry/GPS)
setting.action_space: recommends continuous state spaces; AI2-THOR scenarios use discrete Move Forward/Backward, Rotate Left/Right (+Look Up/Down, Open/Close X for ObjectGoal), Terminate; Gibson action space is user-defined (discrete or continuous); a DONE/stop action is required
setting.simulator: standard scenarios for MINOS (SUNCG, Matterport3D), AI2-THOR, Gibson
setting.privileged: none (recommends explicitly quantifying any prior exposure / perfect odometry)

numbers_note: No experimental results: this is a consensus methodology paper that defines SPL, evaluation recommendations and standard scenario splits, and reports no agent performance numbers.
results: No empirical results. The contributions are seven recommendations: DONE action, geodesic distance, SPL as primary metric, continuous state spaces, SI units, sim-to-real deployment software, and study of internal representations. It also releases standard scenario splits for SUNCG, Matterport3D, AI2-THOR and Gibson. SPL and the stop-action/geodesic success criterion became the de facto standard for PointNav, ObjectNav and VLN evaluation.
limitations: No empirical validation: the paper runs no baselines or human studies, so the suggested 'SPL 0.5 is good' level is not calibrated.

SPL counts only path length and binary success. It ignores rotations, time, energy and collisions (these are only listed as auxiliary measures), and its hard threshold τ makes the score discontinuous near the goal.
Standard scenarios depend on specific datasets and simulator versions (e.g., SUNCG, AI2-THOR v1.0). The paper deliberately recommends neither a particular simulator nor an agent representation.
